extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; scientists and educated lay readers (members/attendees of scientific associations)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for reporting on scientific meetings, reviewing scientific books, and describing experimental inventions in a popular-science magazine. Emphasizes what makes meetings, books, experiments, and reports valuable to both scientific and educated general audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific meeting success metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of a successful scientific meeting include large numbers of original papers entered for reading, high registration and attendance (including many new members), and productive scientific work achieved during the sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also noted as indicators: creation of surplus funds to support research; broad participation across sections; the meeting being the largest held; substantive scientific contributions and a strong spirit of investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospitality and local arrangements as part of meeting success
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of local hospitality and arrangements (cordial and profuse hospitalities, entertainments, free excursions, well-provided collation, invitations to local institutions) is an important part of the experience and success of the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-organized committees, completeness of smooth-working arrangements, and suitable social offerings (excursions, visits to institutions) contribute to attendee satisfaction and the meeting's positive public impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of social enjoyment and legitimate scientific work
rubrics_metrics.description: While social enjoyment is a cardinal object of scientific associations, it is also objected that too much time may be spent socially at the expense of scientific work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Management should regulate the social element so as to economize time and minimally hinder legitimate scientific work — preserving social benefits without impairing the meeting's scientific productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for migratory (movable) scientific associations
rubrics_metrics.description: A movable scientific association (holding meetings in different localities) is effective for systematizing research, bringing large numbers of scientific men together annually, and exerting public influence in many parts of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In large countries with widely distributed scientists, itinerant meetings meet requirements better than a single central headquarters; mobility increases accessibility and encourages cooperative relations among scattered workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of an exemplary presidential/scientific address
rubrics_metrics.description: A model discourse reports the present state of knowledge upon a subject of grave interest and is written in a style suited to readers of general intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The address should be able, interesting, and intelligible to a broad educated audience while accurately summarizing advances and perspectives in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and mathematical-symbolic method in logical works (Boole)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boole's logical writings are praised for wholly novel views of logical method and for applying the symbols and operations of mathematics to logic and the laws of thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mature statement of his views is in the larger work ('An Investigation of the Laws of Thought'); incomplete later editions/manuscripts can limit the utility of follow-up publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate audience and use-case for abstruse mathematical works
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mathematical and logical works are too abstruse for use as school textbooks, even at high grades; however, as works of reference they are invaluable to advanced students and specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such works should be recommended as reference material for advanced study rather than elementary instruction; their readership is advanced students and 'special cultivators' of the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental demonstration and interpretation for novel devices (photophone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental reporting should show the principle and mechanism (e.g., photophone: light/radiant-force interaction with selenium producing sounds), include experiments that elucidate and bring the contrivance into shape, and note material properties (selenium's light-sensitive electrical relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful description of observed phenomena (what is transmitted, what intercepts/permits transmission), discussion of likely mechanisms (e.g., a dark ray accompanying light), and cautious judgement on practical usefulness are required; replication and further experimental inquiry are encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a good scientific manual/textbook for general use
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable manual should make universal claims of importance, be suitable for introduction into colleges, high schools, and normal schools, and not be reduced to mere mechanical recitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject matter should arrest attention, be connected with observations and experiments to give reality to acquired knowledge, and be accessible to general readers while including necessary technicalities for advanced use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of methods required for the science of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of mind requires combining three modes: subjective (introspection), objective (outward expressions), and organic (study of brain/nervous structures — neurology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true science of mind necessitates integrating these departments; treatment should relate subjective and objective psychology to organic conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of diagrams and necessity of direct observation in scientific pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams are profuse and helpful but cannot replace direct contact with the real objects they represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students and teachers should encourage direct observation (brains and nervous parts available for study), form classes to master portions of the material, and use diagrams as aids rather than substitutes for hands-on or real-object familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for evaluating evolutionary hypotheses (degeneration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating degeneration as an evolutionary process should rely on evidence such as recapitulative development (embryonic stages reflecting ancestors) and concrete cases (e.g., ship's barnacle, ascidian phallusia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider conditions that predispose to degeneration (parasitism, fixity/immobility, vegetative nutrition, excessive reduction of size); conclusions should be balanced — acknowledging both progressive and retrogressive trends in evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics and noteworthy observations for government scientific surveys/reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Important measures of progress in topographic/hydrographic surveys include triangulation completion and connections, erection of triangulation stations, water-level observations, determination of longitudes/latitudes for key points, completion of charts, and new physical observations (e.g., sand-waves in rivers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports should record quantitative details (e.g., sand-wave speed, crest-to-crest length, height from valley to crest) and note novel or unprecedented observations that affect understanding of the surveyed system.
